svg.title: The eight TOGAF ADM phases as an iterative ring around requirements management, with phase D as the network designer's home ground
svg.desc: Eight phases sit on a dashed ring: A architecture vision, B business architecture, C information systems architecture, D technology architecture, E opportunities and solutions, F migration planning, G implementation governance and H architecture change management. The ring runs back to A, which is what makes the method iterative rather than waterfall. Requirements management sits in the middle and spans every phase. Three notes on the right explain that phase D is where network design lands, that a design must trace back to B and C or it has no basis, and that TOGAF will never choose between spine-leaf and three-tier. A red note ties this to case 1, where phases A and B were skipped and the CFO's three questions went unanswered.
svg.text: TOGAF ADM: a ring, not a waterfall, with requirements held in the middle
Phase D is where a network design lands; phases A to C are what keeps it from landing on nothing
requirements
management
spans every phase
A · vision
B · business
C · information
D · technology
E · solutions
F · migration
G · governance
H · change
H runs back into A: the architecture keeps moving with the business
D is your home ground
Technology architecture is the phase where the network design
is written down: baseline and target, gaps, and the standards
later projects are supposed to obey.
E to H are then delivery mechanics: work packages, roadmap, oversight, change
Trace back or the design has no basis
A design that cannot name the B capability it serves and the C data
and application it connects is a preference, not an architecture.
B → C → D is the whole of “top-down” in one line.
And it will not choose your topology
TOGAF never says spine-leaf or three-tier; that comes from a
reference architecture (SAFE, CVD) and your own constraints.
Case 1: four months in D, and the CFO’s three questions still had no answer.
Skipping A and B is the most expensive shortcut in the chapter: it does not save four weeks, it spends four months on a design that cannot be defended.
